---
title: "Preface"
---

Music theory for people who already write code.

This book assumes we are at ease with arrays, functions, maps, and threads, and
that we cannot read a note. Those two facts together are unusual enough that
most music teaching serves us badly. Beginner material spends chapters on things
we grasped in a paragraph. Reference material assumes a decade of notation we
never acquired.

Sonic Pi closes the gap. It is a live coding environment where music is written
as Ruby, so every musical idea here arrives as something we run, hear, and then
take apart.

## How the course works

Each lesson takes one musical idea, encodes it as data, plays it, and asks for
one change so we can hear what the change did. The programming stays
deliberately ahead of the theory, and our existing skills carry the load.

- **Sound first, name second.** We hear an interval, a cadence, a mode before
  anyone tells us what it is called.
- **Music is data.** A note event carries pitch, onset, duration, amplitude, and
  articulation. Everything else is a function over those.
- **Score and renderer stay separate.** The composition is content. The playback
  function is interpretation. Changing one should not touch the other.
- **Every lesson ends with something worth hearing.** If the last snippet in a
  lesson is a bare test tone, the lesson is broken.
- **Notation arrives late and on demand.** We meet the staff after pitch and
  duration are already familiar as numbers, which turns it into a decoding
  exercise rather than a wall.
- **Ear training runs in parallel.** Ten minutes most days, using drills we wrote
  ourselves, from Part 2 onwards.

## What this is not

This is not the [Sonic Pi tutorial](https://sonic-pi.net/tutorial.html). That one
teaches programming and uses music as the reward, and it is good at that. Here
the programming is assumed. Ruby idioms get a short note the first time they
appear and no more than that, collected in
[Ruby for non-Rubyists](appendix/ruby-for-non-rubyists.qmd) for anyone arriving
from another language.

It is also not a substitute for playing an instrument. Nothing here teaches our
hands anything. What it teaches is what musicians are doing and why, in a
representation we can inspect.

## Working rhythm

Four sessions a week covers the 58 lessons in about fifteen weeks, with the
capstones after that.

| Session | Length | What |
|---|---|---|
| Two per week | 25 to 35 min | New lessons, in order. |
| One per week | 30 min | Consolidation. Reread the last four lessons and rebuild one example from memory. |
| One per week | 30 min | Free play. Use only what we have learned so far and make something we like. |
| Most days | 10 min | Ear drills from our own `drills.rb`. |

Every fourth week, add no new theory. Finish a transcription instead. Theory
sticks when we use it under pressure, and the pressure comes from wanting the
thing to sound right.
